title: Union-Find
summary: Union-Find, or a disjoint set union, keeps groups that only ever merge. Each group is a tree with one root; find walks to the root, and union hangs one root under the other.
idea: parent[x] points towards x's root. find(x) follows it, halving the path as it goes. union(a, b) hangs the smaller root under the larger, so trees stay shallow.

signals.see: Pairs arrive one at a time and you must keep track of which items are in the same group.
signals.think: Union each pair as it arrives. Two items are in the same group exactly when find gives the same root.

signals.see: Find the edge that creates a cycle, or check whether adding an edge joins two separate groups.
signals.think: Before uniting a and b, compare find(a) and find(b). Equal roots mean they were already connected, so this edge closes a cycle.

signals.see: Count groups as they merge, such as accounts sharing an email or islands appearing one by one.
signals.think: Start with n groups and subtract one each time a union actually joins two different roots.

phrasings: Network cables are added one by one. Which cable is the first to connect two machines that were already connected?
Accounts that share any email belong to one person. Merge them.
Land appears on a grid cell by cell. After each addition, how many islands are there?

picture.title: Relabelling groups versus linking roots
picture.alt: On the left, merging two groups relabels every member of one group, which can cost O(n) per merge. On the right, each group is a tree; merging hangs one root under the other in O(1), and find with path halving keeps trees almost flat.
picture.caption: Union by size plus path compression makes each operation nearly constant time.

code.py:
def count_groups(n, edges):
    parent, size = list(range(n)), [1] * n  #@init
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]  #@hop
        return x  #@root
    groups = n
    for a, b in edges:
        ra, rb = find(a), find(b)  #@edge
        if ra == rb: continue  #@same
        if size[ra] < size[rb]: ra, rb = rb, ra  #@size
        parent[rb] = ra; size[ra] += size[rb]; groups -= 1  #@union
    return groups  #@done

visualiser.inputHelp: n is 2 to 8 nodes, numbered from 0. List up to 12 edges like 0-1, 1-2; each pair at most once.

oneLiner: find: follow parent to the root, halving the path; union: if roots differ, hang the smaller under the larger

exercise.prompt: An office has n computers numbered 0 to n − 1 and some cables, each joining two computers. You may unplug any cable and plug it between any two computers. Return the fewest moves to connect every computer, or -1 if there are not enough cables. The starter never checks whether there are enough cables.
hints: A network of n computers needs at least n − 1 cables. With fewer, the answer is -1.
Otherwise, count the separate groups with Union-Find. Each move can join one more group, so the answer is groups − 1.

complexity.why: With union by size and path halving, each find takes amortised α(V) steps, the inverse Ackermann function, which is under 5 for any real input. The parent and size arrays hold one entry per node.

mistakes: Setting parent[a] = b instead of linking the roots, which breaks the trees.
Comparing parent[a] with parent[b] instead of find(a) with find(b).
Skipping both union by size and path compression, so a long chain makes find O(n).
Counting a group merge even when the two items already shared a root.

quiz.question: When do two items belong to the same group?
choices: When a and b are adjacent
quiz.explain: Only the roots identify a group; direct parents can differ inside one tree.

quiz.question: Edges are added one by one. How do you spot the first one that creates a cycle?
choices: Before uniting, check whether both ends already have the same root
quiz.explain: Equal roots mean the ends were already connected, so the new edge closes a loop.

quiz.question: Why hang the smaller tree under the larger root?
choices: It keeps trees shallow, so find stays fast
quiz.explain: Union by size stops long chains from forming. The answer stays correct without it, but slower.

interviewTip: Write find and union as two short functions first and mention path compression and union by size by name. Interviewers often ask for the complexity, and 'nearly constant, inverse Ackermann' is the expected answer.
